title: MCP Goes Stateless: The 2026-07-28 Specification
content:
## Overview

On July 28, 2026, the Model Context Protocol steering committee published the **2026-07-28 specification** — described by the project's own blog as the most substantial revision to MCP since authorization was added. The headline change: MCP's protocol core is now **stateless**, achieved through six coordinated Specification Enhancement Proposals (SEPs) rather than a single breaking rewrite.

This page covers what changed and why it matters for anyone running or building MCP servers (including the servers Claude Code connects to, like the ones listed in this session's tool set).

---

## Why Statelessness

Earlier MCP versions modeled a server connection like a long-lived session: a client opens a connection, initializes capabilities, and keeps that connection pinned for the life of the interaction. This works for a single desktop client talking to a local server over stdio, but it breaks down for the deployments that now dominate real usage — servers fronted by load balancers, deployed across multiple replicas, or accessed by many short-lived agent processes (exactly the shape of a Claude Code or Claude Agent SDK fleet spinning up workflow subagents). A stateful handshake pinned to one server instance doesn't survive a request landing on a different replica.

The 2026-07-28 spec removes that requirement at the protocol layer: each request carries what it needs to be handled by any replica, without server-side session affinity.

---

## What's New

- **Stateless protocol core** — session state is no longer implicit in a pinned connection; clients and servers exchange enough context per-request to make any replica interchangeable.
- **Multi Round-Trip Requests** — a single logical operation can span more than one request/response exchange, useful for long-running tool calls that previously had to be modeled as fire-and-forget or polled out-of-band.
- **Header-based routing** — routing metadata moves into transport headers instead of being baked into the JSON-RPC payload, simplifying how gateways and proxies direct traffic.
- **Cacheable list results** — `tools/list`, `resources/list`, and similar enumeration calls can now be cached with standard HTTP semantics, cutting redundant round-trips for clients (like Claude Code) that re-discover a server's tools on every session start.
- **Authorization hardening** — tightens edge cases in the OAuth-based authorization flow introduced in earlier 2025 revisions.
- **Formal extensions framework** — a structured way for vendors to ship non-standard capabilities without forking the spec, replacing ad hoc vendor fields.

---

## Enterprise-Managed Authorization

The **Enterprise-Managed Authorization** extension, built on the new extensions framework, reached stable status alongside the July spec. It lets an organization centralize authorization for every MCP server it uses, so end users authenticate once and that single login grants access across all connected servers — rather than authorizing each MCP server individually. Anthropic, Microsoft, and Okta are adopting it, alongside a growing set of third-party MCP servers.

---

## Adoption Scale

By mid-2026, MCP's Tier 1 SDKs (TypeScript and Python) are each seeing roughly half a billion downloads per month, and both have individually crossed 1 billion total downloads. That scale is part of why the steering committee chose a staged SEP process for the stateless transition instead of a single flag-day break — production deployments needed a migration path, not a cliff.

---

## Practical Note for MCP Server Authors

Servers built against pre-2026-07-28 clients should still function — the spec was designed to allow incremental adoption — but authors relying on server-side session state (e.g., storing per-connection context in memory keyed by a session object) should plan to move that state into the request payload or an external store, since a future revision may deprecate the stateful fallback entirely.
